abstract: Summary Cancers and neurodegenerative disorders are associated with both disrupted proteostasis and altered nuclear morphology. Determining if changes in nuclear morphology contribute to pathology requires an understanding of the underlying mechanisms, which are difficult to elucidate in cells where pleiotropic effects of altering proteostasis might indirectly influence nuclear morphology. To investigate direct effects, we studied nuclei assembled in Xenopus egg extract where potentially confounding effects of transcription, translation, cell cycle progression, and actin dynamics are absent. We report that proteasome inhibition causes acute microtubule-dependent changes in nuclear morphology and stability and altered microtubule dynamics and organization. Proteomic analysis of proteasome-inhibited extracts identified an increased abundance of microtubule nucleator TubGCP6, and TubGCP6 depletion partially rescued nuclear morphology. Key results were confirmed in HeLa cells. We propose that accumulation of TubGCP6 leads to altered microtubule dynamics proximal to the nucleus, producing forces that deform the nucleus and impact nuclear morphology and integrity.

Method details
Xenopus
egg extracts, nuclear assembly, extract treatments, and live imaging
Metaphase-arrested
Xenopus laevis
egg extracts were prepared as previously described.
84
Briefly, freshly laid eggs were dejellied and crushed by centrifugation. Cytoplasmic extract was supplemented with 10 μg/mL each leupeptin, pepstatin, and chymostatin, 0.1 mg/mL cytochalasin D, and energy mix (3.8 mM creatine phosphate disodium, 0.5 mM ATP disodium salt, 0.5 mM MgCl
2
). Demembranated sperm chromatin was prepared as described.
37
,
85
Using freshly prepared extract,
de novo
nuclear assembly was performed by adding 0.6 mM CaCl
2
and 0.15 mg/mL cycloheximide along with demembranated sperm nuclei to a final concentration of 1000/μL.
86
The reaction was incubated at room temperature and a small aliquot was used to test for successful nuclear assembly after 30–45 min. Typically, round import-competent nuclei form within this time frame, however this time varies depending on egg and extract quality. After nuclear assembly, we proceed with small molecule treatments. For proteasome inhibition, extracts containing import-competent nuclei were treated with 500 μM MG132 for 45 min. To inhibit microtubules, 33 μM nocodazole was added. To inhibit NPC-mediated nucleocytoplasmic transport, wheat germ agglutinin (WGA) was added to extracts at a concentration of 2 μg/μL.
For live imaging of nuclear assembly and growth, freshly prepared egg extracts were supplemented with CaCl
2
, cycloheximide, energy mix, and demembranated sperm chromatin as stated above along with 500 μM MG132 or an equivalent volume of buffer as a control. To visualize nuclei, recombinant GST-GFP-NLS
82
was added at a concentration of 0.4 μg/μL. Time-lapse imaging was started immediately, and images were acquired at regular 30 s or 3 min intervals for 1–1.5 h.
Cell culture
HeLa cells were typically grown in T-25 flasks. However, for small molecule treatments and immunofluorescence assays cells were grown in 6-well plates on acid-washed sterile coverslips. For proteasome inhibition, cells were treated with 0.2 mM MG132 for 1 h. To depolymerize microtubule, cells were treated with 3 μM nocodazole 1 h.

Coverslips were mounted on glass slides with Vectashield Mounting Medium (Vector Laboratories, H-1000) and sealed with transparent nail polish.
HeLa cell immunofluorescence assays were performed as described previously.
89
Briefly, cells were grown in 6-well plates on acid-washed sterile cover slips to 70–75% confluency. Cells were washed twice with PBS and then fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde. Cells were washed with PBS and then permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100. Cells were washed with PBS and blocked with 10% goat serum (Sigma, G9023) and 0.3 M glycine in PBS. Primary antibody incubation was performed overnight at 4°C followed by PBS washes and secondary antibody incubation. Antibodies were diluted in 2% goat serum in PBS. Mass spectrometry and DIA analysis
Freshly prepared
X. laevis
egg extracts were supplemented with 0.6 mM CaCl
2
and 0.15 mg/mL cycloheximide to produce interphase-arrested extracts. Extract quality was assessed by using a small aliquot to test for formation of import-competent nuclei. Poor quality extracts were not used for proteomic analysis. Next, interphase extracts were supplemented with 500 μM MG132 or an equivalent volume of buffer for controls and incubated at room temperature for 45 min. Treated extracts were flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and shipped on dry ice to the IDeA National Resource for Quantitative Proteomics (University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences, Little Rock, AR). Total protein from each sample was reduced, alkylated, and purified by chloroform/methanol extraction prior to digestion with sequencing grade modified porcine trypsin (Promega). Tryptic peptides were then separated by reverse phase XSelect CSH C18 2.5 μm resin (Waters) on an in-line 150 × 0.075 mm column using an UltiMate 3000 RSLCnano system (Thermo). Peptides were eluted using a 60 min gradient from 98:2 to 65:35 buffer A:B ratio (Buffer A = 0.1% formic acid, 0.5% acetonitrile, Buffer B = 0.1% formic acid, 99.9% acetonitrile). Eluted peptides were ionized by electrospray (2.2 kV) followed by mass spectrometric analysis on an Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo). To assemble a chromatogram library, six gas-phase fractions were acquired on the Orbitrap Exploris with 4 m/z DIA spectra (4 m/z precursor isolation windows at 30,000 resolution, normalized AGC target 100%, maximum inject time 66 ms) using a staggered window pattern from narrow mass ranges using optimized window placements. Precursor spectra were acquired after each DIA duty cycle, spanning the m/z range of the gas-phase fraction (i.e., 496–602 m/z, 60,000 resolution, normalized AGC target 100%, maximum injection time 50 ms). For wide-window acquisitions, the Orbitrap Exploris was configured to acquire a precursor scan (385–1015 m/z, 60,000 resolution, normalized AGC target 100%, maximum injection time 50 ms) followed by 50 × 12 m/z DIA spectra (12 m/z precursor isolation windows at 15,000 resolution, normalized AGC target 100%, maximum injection time 33 ms) using a staggered window pattern with optimized window placements. Precursor spectra were acquired after each DIA duty cycle. Following data acquisition, data were searched using an empirically corrected library against the UniProt
Xenopus laevis
database (February 2022) and a quantitative analysis was performed to obtain a comprehensive proteomic profile. Proteins were identified and quantified using EncyclopeDIA
93
,
94
and visualized with Scaffold DIA using 1% false discovery thresholds at both the protein and peptide level. Protein MS2 exclusive intensity values were assessed for quality using ProteiNorm.
95
The data were normalized using cyclic loess
96
and analyzed using proteoDA to perform statistical analysis using Linear Models for Microarray Data (limma) with empirical Bayes (eBayes) smoothing to the standard errors.
96
,
97
Proteins with an FDR adjusted
p
-value <0.05 and a fold change >2 were considered significant.
Immunodepletion of extracts
Xenopus
egg extracts were immunodepleted of TubGCP6 as described.
98
Briefly, 100 μL of Protein A Dynabead slurry (Life Technologies, 10001D) were washed with antibody wash/coupling buffer (0.01 M HEPES pH 8, 0.15 M NaCl), resuspended in the same buffer, and incubated with 5 μg of anti-TubGCP6 antibody (ABclonal, A15921) for 1 h. The antibody-bound beads were collected using a magnet and washed thrice with antibody wash/coupling buffer. The washed beads were incubated with 50 μL of freshly prepared
Xenopus
egg extract for 45 min to allow TubGCP6 protein to bind to the beads. The beads were then immobilized using a magnet and the immunodepleted extract was transferred to a fresh tube. Mock depletions were performed as controls. Immunodepleted and mock-depleted extracts were used for
de novo
nuclear assembly, followed by treatment with 500 μM MG132 for 45 min, fixation, and immunofluorescence.
Western blots
Western blot samples included mitotic versus interphase extracts, control versus MG132-treated extracts, and mock versus TubGCP6 immunodepleted extracts. The protein concentration of the extracts was estimated by Bradford assay using BSA standards. Twenty-five μg of total extract protein were mixed with SDS-PAGE loading buffer (0.05% Bromophenol Blue, 0.1 M dithiothreitol, 10% glycerol, 2% SDS, 0.05 M Tris-HCl, pH 6.8) and boiled for 10 min. Proteins were separated on 4–20% Mini-PROTEAN TGX Precast Gels (Bio-Rad) and transferred to Immobilon-FL polyvinylidene difluoride membranes (Merck Millipore, IPFL00010) by wet transfer using Towbin Buffer
99
(2.5 mM Tris, 192 mM Glycine, 20% methanol) at 100 V for 1 h at 4°C. The membrane was cut in two so the top portion could be probed for TubGCP6 and the bottom portion could be probed for actin or tubulin. Blocking was performed with TBS plus 0.05% Tween 20 containing 3% BSA for 2 h at room temperature, followed by overnight incubation at 4°C with the primary antibody diluted in TBS plus 0.05% Tween 20. The membrane was washed three times with TBS plus 0.1% Tween 20 for 5 min each and incubated for 2 h at room temperature with secondary antibody diluted in TBS plus 0.05% Tween 20. The membrane was washed three times with TBS plus 0.1% Tween 20 for 5 min each. After a final TBS rinse, the membrane was imaged using an Odyssey CLx instrument (LI-COR Biosciences). After imaging, the membrane was stained with Ponceau S to estimate the total protein per lane for normalization. Band intensities were quantified using ImageJ/Fiji. The following primary antibodies were used: anti-TubGCP6 antibody at 1:250 (ABclonal, A15921), anti-β-tubulin antibody at 1:1000 (ABclonal, AC008), and anti-β-actin antibody at 1:1000 (Cell Signaling Technology 49700). The secondary antibody was IRDye 800CW anti-rabbit at 1:20,000 (LI-COR Biosciences, 926–32211).
Microscopy and image analysis
Widefield imaging was performed with an Olympus BX63 upright widefield epifluorescence microscope having multi-mode time-lapse imaging ability with an X-Cite 120 LED illumination system. Images were acquired using a high-resolution Hamamatsu ORCA-Flash4.0 digital CMOS camera at room temperature. Confocal microscopy was performed using an Olympus IX83 spinning disk confocal microscope (Yokogawa CSW-W1 SoRA) equipped with an ORCA-Fusion Digital CMOS camera. Olympus objectives included the PLanApoN 2× (NA 0.08, air), UPLanFLN 20X (NA 0.5, air), UPLanSApo 40X (NA 1.25, silicon oil), and UPLanSApo 100X (NA 1.35, silicon oil). A fully motorized Olympus stage was used to position the samples along the x, y, and z axes. Image acquisition and automation were controlled by Olympus CellSens Imaging software and image analysis was performed using ImageJ/Fiji.
83
Thresholded images were used to quantify cross sectional (CS) nuclear area.
84
We have shown previously that CS nuclear area accurately predicts total nuclear surface area and volume.
1
,
2
,
82
,
87
Nuclear roundness, which is the ratio of CS area to the square of the major axis, was calculated from thresholded images using ImageJ/Fiji. We quantified nuclear import and growth rates as previously described,
84
using the first 10 min of live time-lapse imaging after formation of import-competent nuclei. Briefly, nuclei assembled in
Xenopus
egg extract were live imaged for GFP-NLS as described above. Mean nuclear GFP-NLS pixel intensity was measured for each nucleus using ImageJ/Fiji and multiplied by nuclear volume to obtain the total integrated nuclear GFP-NLS signal within the entire volume of the nucleus. These values were plotted as a function of time, and the import rate was calculated from the slope of the graphs. To measure nuclear growth rates, nuclear CS areas from the same time-lapses were quantified and plotted as a function of time. Nuclear growth rate was calculated from the slope of the graphs. To quantify nuclear rupture, it is important to note that the intranuclear GFP-NLS signal disperses upon rupture. To quantify the number of ruptured nuclei, we counted the number of nuclei positive for intranuclear GFP-NLS at the start of imaging and subtracted the number of nuclei still positive for intranuclear GFP-NLS after 1 h. This number was divided by the initial number of nuclei to obtain the rupture frequency. Ruptures typically occurred after the 10-min window used to calculate nuclear growth and import rates. Heterogeneity in nuclear pore complex (NPC) distribution, which reflects the wrinkled appearance of the nuclear envelope, was measured from fixed images using the same principle as described previously.
100
Briefly, using ImageJ/Fiji, line scans were drawn within the nuclear interior and the standard deviation of the NPC signal intensity along the line was calculated. A homogeneous distribution of NPC (and smoother nuclear envelope) produces a smaller SD value compared to the larger SD value for nuclei with a heterogeneous NPC distribution (and wrinkled nuclear envelope). SD values for all line scans were normalized to their average intensities to calculate the heterogeneity of NPC distribution value. To quantify nuclei in control and MG132-treated HeLa cells with or without nocodazole, ImageJ/Fiji
83
was used to threshold images and measure the nuclear CS area and Feret’s diameter, which is a measure of the longest distance between any two points along the selection boundary.
Imaging for aster microtubule architecture and growth dynamics was conducted using an Olympus IX-81 inverted spinning disk confocal microscope with a CSU X1 confocal head (Yokogawa) and an Orca-FLASH 4.0 sCMOS camera (Hamamatsu). A 60× UPlanSApo oil objective (1.35 NA) was used for acquiring images in a temperature-controlled room maintained at 17°C. For time-lapse studies, the initial time point was set when confined aMTOCs started nucleating microtubules upon removal from ice. Imaging to observe microtubule architecture and microtubule plus end growth dynamics was started at the 10-min time point after the microtubule interphase aster reached a steady state. For microtubule pattern imaging (mCherry-TMBD), single z stack images close to the coverslip were captured at 5 s intervals for 2.5 min. For microtubule plus end growth dynamics measurements (EB1-GFP), single z stack images near the coverslip were acquired at 0.5 s intervals for 1 min. To measure the radial distribution of astral microtubules near the aster center, a 10 μm radial zone around the aMTOC was isolated, and the surrounding area was cleared in ImageJ. The "Radial Profile" plugin
101
was then applied to the cropped microtubule image (Gaussian blur; radius = 5). Using the aMTOC coordinates as the center and with a 10 μm radius around the aMTOC, all integrated intensity values were normalized to the peak intensity for the microtubule channel and then plotted against their respective radial distances from the aMTOC. Microtubule growth rates and EB1 comet velocities across the entire enclosure were quantified using u-track particle tracking software version 2.0,
102
as described previously.
63
Briefly, "Microtubule plus-ends" tracking and "Comet Detection" were utilized to identify EB1 comets. Typically, a high-pass Gaussian filter of 7 and a watershed minimum threshold of 5 were applied. A minimum track length of three frames was maintained, and frame-to-frame linking bounds were set at twice the mean growth rate to reduce false linking. No forward reclassification was used. To quantify the EB1 comets near the aster center, a 15 μm radial zone around the aMTOC was cropped, and the area outside this zone was cleared. EB1 comets imaged for 1 min in the selected region near the aMTOC were quantified using u-track particle tracking software. The EB1 comet counts near the aMTOC were recorded and plotted for both control and MG132 treatments.

Freshly prepared
X. laevis

Next, interphase extracts were supplemented with 500 μM MG132 or an equivalent volume of buffer for controls and incubated at room temperature for 45 min. Xenopus laevis
database (February 2022) and a quantitative analysis was performed to obtain a comprehensive proteomic profile. Proteins were identified and quantified using EncyclopeDIA
93
,
94

96

,
97

p
-value <0.05 and a fold change >2 were considered significant.

Microscopy and image analysis
Widefield imaging was performed with an Olympus BX63 upright widefield epifluorescence microscope having multi-mode time-lapse imaging ability with an X-Cite 120 LED illumination system. Images were acquired using a high-resolution Hamamatsu ORCA-Flash4.0 digital CMOS camera at room temperature. Confocal microscopy was performed using an Olympus IX83 spinning disk confocal microscope (Yokogawa CSW-W1 SoRA) equipped with an ORCA-Fusion Digital CMOS camera. Olympus objectives included the PLanApoN 2× (NA 0.08, air), UPLanFLN 20X (NA 0.5, air), UPLanSApo 40X (NA 1.25, silicon oil), and UPLanSApo 100X (NA 1.35, silicon oil). A fully motorized Olympus stage was used to position the samples along the x, y, and z axes. Image acquisition and automation were controlled by Olympus CellSens Imaging software and image analysis was performed using ImageJ/Fiji.
83
Thresholded images were used to quantify cross sectional (CS) nuclear area.
84
We have shown previously that CS nuclear area accurately predicts total nuclear surface area and volume.
1
,
2
,
82
,
87
Nuclear roundness, which is the ratio of CS area to the square of the major axis, was calculated from thresholded images using ImageJ/Fiji. We quantified nuclear import and growth rates as previously described,
84
using the first 10 min of live time-lapse imaging after formation of import-competent nuclei. Briefly, nuclei assembled in
Xenopus
egg extract were live imaged for GFP-NLS as described above. Mean nuclear GFP-NLS pixel intensity was measured for each nucleus using ImageJ/Fiji and multiplied by nuclear volume to obtain the total integrated nuclear GFP-NLS signal within the entire volume of the nucleus. These values were plotted as a function of time, and the import rate was calculated from the slope of the graphs. To measure nuclear growth rates, nuclear CS areas from the same time-lapses were quantified and plotted as a function of time. Nuclear growth rate was calculated from the slope of the graphs. To quantify nuclear rupture, it is important to note that the intranuclear GFP-NLS signal disperses upon rupture. To quantify the number of ruptured nuclei, we counted the number of nuclei positive for intranuclear GFP-NLS at the start of imaging and subtracted the number of nuclei still positive for intranuclear GFP-NLS after 1 h. This number was divided by the initial number of nuclei to obtain the rupture frequency. Ruptures typically occurred after the 10-min window used to calculate nuclear growth and import rates. Heterogeneity in nuclear pore complex (NPC) distribution, which reflects the wrinkled appearance of the nuclear envelope, was measured from fixed images using the same principle as described previously.
100
Briefly, using ImageJ/Fiji, line scans were drawn within the nuclear interior and the standard deviation of the NPC signal intensity along the line was calculated. A homogeneous distribution of NPC (and smoother nuclear envelope) produces a smaller SD value compared to the larger SD value for nuclei with a heterogeneous NPC distribution (and wrinkled nuclear envelope). SD values for all line scans were normalized to their average intensities to calculate the heterogeneity of NPC distribution value. To quantify nuclei in control and MG132-treated HeLa cells with or without nocodazole, ImageJ/Fiji
83
was used to threshold images and measure the nuclear CS area and Feret’s diameter, which is a measure of the longest distance between any two points along the selection boundary.
Imaging for aster microtubule architecture and growth dynamics was conducted using an Olympus IX-81 inverted spinning disk confocal microscope with a CSU X1 confocal head (Yokogawa) and an Orca-FLASH 4.0 sCMOS camera (Hamamatsu). A 60× UPlanSApo oil objective (1.35 NA) was used for acquiring images in a temperature-controlled room maintained at 17°C. For time-lapse studies, the initial time point was set when confined aMTOCs started nucleating microtubules upon removal from ice. Imaging to observe microtubule architecture and microtubule plus end growth dynamics was started at the 10-min time point after the microtubule interphase aster reached a steady state. For microtubule pattern imaging (mCherry-TMBD), single z stack images close to the coverslip were captured at 5 s intervals for 2.5 min. For microtubule plus end growth dynamics measurements (EB1-GFP), single z stack images near the coverslip were acquired at 0.5 s intervals for 1 min. To measure the radial distribution of astral microtubules near the aster center, a 10 μm radial zone around the aMTOC was isolated, and the surrounding area was cleared in ImageJ. The "Radial Profile" plugin
101
was then applied to the cropped microtubule image (Gaussian blur; radius = 5). Using the aMTOC coordinates as the center and with a 10 μm radius around the aMTOC, all integrated intensity values were normalized to the peak intensity for the microtubule channel and then plotted against their respective radial distances from the aMTOC. Microtubule growth rates and EB1 comet velocities across the entire enclosure were quantified using u-track particle tracking software version 2.0,
102
as described previously.
63
Briefly, "Microtubule plus-ends" tracking and "Comet Detection" were utilized to identify EB1 comets. Typically, a high-pass Gaussian filter of 7 and a watershed minimum threshold of 5 were applied. A minimum track length of three frames was maintained, and frame-to-frame linking bounds were set at twice the mean growth rate to reduce false linking. No forward reclassification was used. To quantify the EB1 comets near the aster center, a 15 μm radial zone around the aMTOC was cropped, and the area outside this zone was cleared. EB1 comets imaged for 1 min in the selected region near the aMTOC were quantified using u-track particle tracking software. The EB1 comet counts near the aMTOC were recorded and plotted for both control and MG132 treatments.

Introduction
Organelle size and shape influence organelle and cell function. A fundamental question in cell biology is how nuclear morphology is regulated. Under normal physiological conditions, nuclear size typically scales with cell size to maintain a constant nuclear-to-cytoplasmic volume ratio.
1
,
2
,
3
,
4
In general, nuclei are roughly spherical although there are variations in nuclear shape based on cell type, species, and differentiation status.
5
,
6
,
7
In diseased conditions including many cancers and laminopathies, significant aberrations in nuclear size and shape occur.
6
,
7
,
8
,
9
,
10
,
11
,
12
,
13
,
14
Alterations in nuclear morphology can affect biological processes like cell migration and gene expression,
5
,
15
,
16
,
17
,
18
however, it is generally unclear how nuclear morphology influences cell function, necessitating a more complete understanding of the underlying mechanisms.
Some regulators of nuclear morphology have been identified.
5
Intranuclear factors include the nuclear lamina, nucleoporins, and chromatin modifications whereas the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and cytoskeleton are extranuclear factors that contribute to the regulation of nuclear size and shape.
5
,
15
,
17
,
19
,
20
,
21
,
22
,
23
,
24
,
25
One essential aspect of cellular function that could influence nuclear morphology but has received relatively little attention is protein turnover.
26
,
27
Protein homeostasis or proteostasis maintains proteins at their correct concentrations while ensuring that misfolded, aged, and damaged proteins are removed from the cellular protein pool.
28
,
29
,
30
,
31
One of the major pathways by which proteostasis is maintained and proteotoxicity is avoided is the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS). In eukaryotes the UPS is the primary route by which proteins are eliminated whereby polyubiquitinated proteins are targeted to the proteasome for degradation.
32
Aberrations in proteostasis and the UPS contribute to a variety of diseases including many cancers and neurodegenerative diseases.
33
Interestingly, nuclear morphology is often altered in these same disease states.
34
,
35
,
36
It is unknown if defects in proteostasis directly cause changes in nuclear morphology, a key issue when considering disease mechanisms and therapies.
One approach to studying aberrant proteostasis is to inhibit the proteasome. However, pleiotropy associated with proteasome inhibition in intact cells makes it difficult to discern direct effects on any one cell biological process. To minimize these potentially confounding effects, we studied the effect of short-term proteasome inhibition on nuclear morphology using the
Xenopus
egg extract system that supports
de novo
nuclear assembly. Major advantages of this approach are that there is no transcription, new protein synthesis, cell cycle progression, or dynamic actin in our extract preparations, thus any effects we observe are independent of these major regulators of cellular function.
37
,
38
,
39
,
40
Upon short-term inhibition of the proteasome,
41
we observed acute changes in nuclear morphology and stability mediated in part by changes in microtubule dynamics and the level of a key regulator of microtubule nucleation. Our data support a model whereby proteasome inhibition directly enhances microtubule dynamics proximal to the nucleus, producing forces that deform the nucleus and impact nuclear morphology and integrity.
Results and discussion
Proteasome inhibitor MG132 affects nuclear morphology
We made use of
Xenopus laevis
egg extracts that are transcriptionally inert and treated with cytochalasin to depolymerize actin. Mitotic extracts were driven into interphase and treated with cycloheximide to inhibit protein translation and induce interphase arrest.
38
Xenopus
sperm chromatin was added to promote
de novo
nuclear assembly, and extracts were also supplemented with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 or an equivalent volume of buffer as a control. Import-competent nuclei typically form after 30–45 min. Live imaging of imported GFP-NLS performed during nuclear assembly showed that the nuclear growth rate was significantly reduced in the presence of MG132 (
Figures 1
A–1C and 1E). We also quantified nuclear import rates as the integrated volumetric increase in nuclear GFP-NLS signal over time. Nuclear import rates were unaffected by MG132 (
Figures 1
D and 1F), indicating that reduced nuclear growth did not result from an import defect. Additionally, nuclear integrity was compromised in the presence of MG132 as evidenced by an increase in the frequency of nuclear rupture (
Figure 1
G and
Video S1
).

Next, we treated pre-assembled nuclei with MG132 for 45 min and quantified the morphology of fixed nuclei, finding that nuclei in MG132-treated extracts were smaller and less round (
Figures 1

42
,
43
While WGA-treated nuclei were smaller than controls due to blocked nuclear import, WGA-treated nuclei incubated with MG132 showed a further reduction in nuclear size (
Figures S1
A–S1B). We also noted that MG132-treated nuclei exhibited a wrinkled appearance which could be quantified as a more heterogeneous distribution of NPCs (
Figures S1
A and S1C). This same increase in NPC heterogeneity was also observed for WGA-treated nuclei (
Figures S1

While our experiments in
Xenopus

We subjected HeLa cells that were CRISPR modified to express GFP-Lamin A (eGFP-LMNA)
44
to MG132 treatment for 1 h, reasoning that this acute treatment might reveal direct effects on nuclear morphology. Nuclei in MG132-treated cells were smaller (
Figures 1

49
Indeed, Feret’s diameters in HeLa cell nuclei treated with MG132 were significantly smaller as compared to controls (
Figures 1

Microtubules contribute to MG132-induced nuclear morphology changes
Given that microtubules have been implicated in the regulation of nuclear morphology,
50
,
51
,
52
,
53
,
54
we next tested if microtubule depolymerization with nocodazole
55
could rescue MG132-induced nuclear morphology defects. Import-competent nuclei assembled in
X. laevis
egg extract were treated with MG132 in the presence or absence of nocodazole for 45 min. The reduced size of MG132-treated nuclei was partially rescued upon microtubule depolymerization (
Figures 2

Figures 2

,
57
,
58

Figures 2

Figures 2

59
,
60
,
61
that leads to altered nuclear morphology, a reduction in nuclear growth, and an increase in the frequency of nuclear rupture. In turn, these effects on nuclear integrity might explain why average nuclear size is reduced and nuclei adopt a wrinkled appearance with a more heterogeneous NPC distribution.

If an overabundance of TubGCP6 in MG132-treated extracts was leading to small, misshapen nuclei, then we predicted that reducing the level of TubGCP6 would rescue nuclear morphology. We immunodepleted TubGCP6 from extracts (
Figures S3
E–S3F), performed nuclear assembly, and then treated extracts with MG132 or a buffer control. Whereas mock depleted extracts treated with MG132 produced small nuclei compared to controls, this MG132-induced effect was partially rescued in TubGCP6-depleted extracts in which nuclei approached the size of untreated nuclei in mock depleted extract (
Figures 4
C and 4D). Interestingly, in the absence of MG132, nuclear size was increased in TubGCP6-depleted extracts compared to mock depleted extracts, implicating TubGCP6 as a more general negative regulator of nuclear size (

Figures 4
C and 4E). Taken together, we have identified proteins whose abundance increases in extract upon proteasome inhibition and shown that increased levels of TubGCP6 contribute to MG132-induced changes in nuclear morphology.
Based on our data, we propose a model whereby proteasome inhibition leads to an overabundance TubGCP6 that increases microtubule nucleation activity at the centrosome. These altered microtubule dynamics in close proximity to the nucleus might generate forces that deform the nucleus, accounting for observed changes in nuclear morphology as well as an increased rate of nuclear rupture, akin to the role that microtubules play during mitotic nuclear envelope breakdown.

,

This can also explain why MG132-treated nuclei are smaller with a more wrinkled appearance. Importantly, TubGCP6 depletion and microtubule depolymerization do not fully rescue nuclear morphology, so it will be interesting to explore the contributions of other proteins whose levels remain higher upon proteasome inhibition.
In further characterizing TubGCP6, we also found that TubGCP6 levels are cell cycle regulated, being about 2-fold higher in mitosis compared to interphase (
Figures S3
A–S3B). We hypothesize that higher TubGCP6 levels in mitosis might produce the dynamic microtubules required for spindle assembly.
76
,
77
Then, proteasome-mediated degradation of TubGCP6 in interphase would ensure a reduction in microtubule dynamics that would prevent significant nuclear deformation yet suffice to promote ER network formation and nuclear assembly. This model is consistent with a previous study showing that a balance of microtubule dynamics is critical to achieve normal nuclear morphology, with chromatin-bound Dppa2 inhibiting an excess of microtubules during nuclear assembly.
54
Our data suggest that TubGCP6 levels may be an important physiological regulator of both mitotic spindle assembly and normal interphase nuclear morphology and integrity.
Our study provides mechanistic insight into the effect of short-term proteasome inhibition on nuclear morphology, nuclear integrity, and microtubule dynamics. Proteasome inhibition is known to cause proteotoxic stress, so it will now be interesting to apply our findings to disease states associated with both proteotoxic stress and altered nuclear structure. Are TubGCP6 levels and microtubule dynamics altered in these diseases? Does manipulating microtubule dynamics rescue nuclear morphology defects? How does altered nuclear morphology affect nuclear function and does this contribute to disease pathology? These broad questions will be important areas for future investigation.
Limitations of the study
In the current study, we focused on one candidate protein identified from the proteomics, TubGCP6. Future studies of other candidates might reveal additional mechanisms responsible for MG132-induced changes in nuclear morphology and integrity. Similarly, while our data are consistent with the idea that MG132 treatment leads to an increase in microtubule nucleation, we cannot rule out alternative hypotheses such as MG132-induced changes in cytoplasmic viscosity or levels of microtubule-associated proteins that might account for observed effects on microtubule dynamics. Some aspects of our model remain to be fully elucidated. With respect to proteasomal degradation of TubGCP6, which ubiquitin ligase acts on TubGCP6 and which sites on TubGCP6 are polyubiquitinated? With respect to microtubule-dependent changes in nuclear morphology, how does increased microtubule nucleation lead to deformation and rupture of the nuclear envelope and what are the mechanical forces that are involved? Lastly, while we have shown that microtubules contribute to MG132-induced nuclear morphology changes in HeLa cells, it remains to be seen if this effect is mediated by TubGCP6, although pleiotropic effects of manipulating TubGCP6 levels in cells may make those experiments difficult to interpret.

Next, interphase extracts were supplemented with 500 μM MG132 or an equivalent volume of buffer for controls and incubated at room temperature for 45 min. To assemble a chromatogram library, six gas-phase fractions were acquired on the Orbitrap Exploris with 4 m/z DIA spectra (4 m/z precursor isolation windows at 30,000 resolution, normalized AGC target 100%, maximum inject time 66 ms) using a staggered window pattern from narrow mass ranges using optimized window placements. Nuclear roundness, which is the ratio of CS area to the square of the major axis, was calculated from thresholded images using ImageJ/Fiji. We quantified nuclear import and growth rates as previously described,
84
using the first 10 min of live time-lapse imaging after formation of import-competent nuclei. Briefly, nuclei assembled in
Xenopus
egg extract were live imaged for GFP-NLS as described above. Mean nuclear GFP-NLS pixel intensity was measured for each nucleus using ImageJ/Fiji and multiplied by nuclear volume to obtain the total integrated nuclear GFP-NLS signal within the entire volume of the nucleus. These values were plotted as a function of time, and the import rate was calculated from the slope of the graphs. To measure nuclear growth rates, nuclear CS areas from the same time-lapses were quantified and plotted as a function of time. Nuclear growth rate was calculated from the slope of the graphs. To quantify nuclear rupture, it is important to note that the intranuclear GFP-NLS signal disperses upon rupture. To quantify the number of ruptured nuclei, we counted the number of nuclei positive for intranuclear GFP-NLS at the start of imaging and subtracted the number of nuclei still positive for intranuclear GFP-NLS after 1 h. This number was divided by the initial number of nuclei to obtain the rupture frequency. Ruptures typically occurred after the 10-min window used to calculate nuclear growth and import rates. Heterogeneity in nuclear pore complex (NPC) distribution, which reflects the wrinkled appearance of the nuclear envelope, was measured from fixed images using the same principle as described previously.
100
Briefly, using ImageJ/Fiji, line scans were drawn within the nuclear interior and the standard deviation of the NPC signal intensity along the line was calculated. A homogeneous distribution of NPC (and smoother nuclear envelope) produces a smaller SD value compared to the larger SD value for nuclei with a heterogeneous NPC distribution (and wrinkled nuclear envelope). SD values for all line scans were normalized to their average intensities to calculate the heterogeneity of NPC distribution value. To quantify nuclei in control and MG132-treated HeLa cells with or without nocodazole, ImageJ/Fiji
83
was used to threshold images and measure the nuclear CS area and Feret’s diameter, which is a measure of the longest distance between any two points along the selection boundary.
Imaging for aster microtubule architecture and growth dynamics was conducted using an Olympus IX-81 inverted spinning disk confocal microscope with a CSU X1 confocal head (Yokogawa) and an Orca-FLASH 4.0 sCMOS camera (Hamamatsu). A 60× UPlanSApo oil objective (1.35 NA) was used for acquiring images in a temperature-controlled room maintained at 17°C. For time-lapse studies, the initial time point was set when confined aMTOCs started nucleating microtubules upon removal from ice. Imaging to observe microtubule architecture and microtubule plus end growth dynamics was started at the 10-min time point after the microtubule interphase aster reached a steady state. For microtubule pattern imaging (mCherry-TMBD), single z stack images close to the coverslip were captured at 5 s intervals for 2.5 min. For microtubule plus end growth dynamics measurements (EB1-GFP), single z stack images near the coverslip were acquired at 0.5 s intervals for 1 min. To measure the radial distribution of astral microtubules near the aster center, a 10 μm radial zone around the aMTOC was isolated, and the surrounding area was cleared in ImageJ. The "Radial Profile" plugin
101
was then applied to the cropped microtubule image (Gaussian blur; radius = 5). Using the aMTOC coordinates as the center and with a 10 μm radius around the aMTOC, all integrated intensity values were normalized to the peak intensity for the microtubule channel and then plotted against their respective radial distances from the aMTOC. Microtubule growth rates and EB1 comet velocities across the entire enclosure were quantified using u-track particle tracking software version 2.0,
102
as described previously.
63
Briefly, "Microtubule plus-ends" tracking and "Comet Detection" were utilized to identify EB1 comets. Typically, a high-pass Gaussian filter of 7 and a watershed minimum threshold of 5 were applied. A minimum track length of three frames was maintained, and frame-to-frame linking bounds were set at twice the mean growth rate to reduce false linking. No forward reclassification was used. To quantify the EB1 comets near the aster center, a 15 μm radial zone around the aMTOC was cropped, and the area outside this zone was cleared. EB1 comets imaged for 1 min in the selected region near the aMTOC were quantified using u-track particle tracking software. The EB1 comet counts near the aMTOC were recorded and plotted for both control and MG132 treatments.
